one_line_reason: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses show oral royal jelly benefits postmenopausal symptoms, MASLD, and multiple sclerosis oxidative-stress markers, though glycemic/diabetes claims are directly contradicted between reviews.

selected.population: postmenopausal women (meta-analysis, 6 studies/471 women overall; primary pooled estimate from 2 studies/312 participants)
selected.primary_outcome: postmenopausal symptoms (genitourinary symptoms, quality of life)
selected.why_selected: most recent (2026) and most directly relevant meta-analysis, showing a significant, moderate-quality improvement over placebo.

selected.population: adults (meta-analysis, 5 RCTs; 205 participants for FPG, 130 for HbA1c)
selected.intervention: royal jelly ingestion, oral, vs. placebo
selected.why_selected: a rigorous, quantitative meta-analysis directly concluding royal jelly does NOT significantly improve glycemic markers, an important counterpoint to diabetes-related marketing claims for this ingredient.

selected.population: postmenopausal women with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) (n=23, semi-experimental, randomized)
selected.intervention: royal jelly supplement plus 8 weeks of aerobic-resistance training, oral, vs. exercise plus placebo
selected.dose_as_stated: 500 mg on training days, before each session
selected.primary_outcome: paraoxonase 1 (PON1), oxidized LDL, lipid profile, liver enzymes (ALT, AST)
selected.why_selected: isolates royal jelly's own added effect on top of an identical exercise program in both arms, with a clear dose and multiple significant metabolic/liver improvements.

selected.population: patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (n=61, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled)
selected.primary_outcome: disability score (EDSS), oxidative stress (MDA) and antioxidant markers (SOD, CAT), fatigue and quality of life
selected.why_selected: clean single-ingredient RCT with a clear dose showing significant reductions in disability score and oxidative stress markers, in a different (neurological) clinical population.

blockers: No dose is given for the menopause meta-analysis (41401249) or the broader cardiometabolic umbrella review; only the MASLD and MS RCTs specify a 500 mg/day dose, so mapping potency/standardization to catalog labels is uncertain.

Evidence for glycemic/diabetes outcomes is directly conflicting between sources in this same shortlist (a narrative review reporting benefit vs. a quantitative meta-analysis finding no significant effect), so any diabetes-related claim needs separate, careful adjudication.
The MASLD RCT combines royal jelly with a structured 8-week exercise program in both arms, so its real-world effect without supervised exercise is unconfirmed.

This identity's own shortlist includes a pharmacovigilance review reporting severe asthma attacks and other allergic reactions after royal jelly consumption, a relevant safety consideration given it is a bee product.

handoff_pmids.note: Pharmacovigilance/toxicology review of apitherapy products; reports cases of severe asthma attacks following royal jelly consumption, among other bee-product adverse events, particularly in atopic individuals.

excluded_pmids.reason: Narrative literature review of royal jelly's hormonal effects in breast cancer; the supporting data are mostly preclinical (animal doses in mg/kg), and the authors explicitly state future clinical studies are needed before any human dosing conclusion.

Narrative review of multiple bee products (honey, pollen, royal jelly, propolis) together for PCOS-related infertility; states clinical trial data are limited and does not isolate royal jelly's own effect.

Narrative systematic review reporting royal jelly improves glycemic and lipid markers in diabetes; conflicts with and is less rigorous than the quantitative meta-analysis already selected (31126561), which found no significant glycemic effect.

Meta-analysis of royal jelly on liver enzymes and glycemic indices finding an overall null result (with one small subgroup exception); redundant with the glycemic null finding already captured by the selected meta-analysis (31126561).
Review comparing apitherapy books' claims about allergic rhinitis to the scientific literature for bee products generally; not focused on royal jelly's own efficacy data.
Review of oral mucositis prevention/treatment listing royal jelly among several effective options without any royal-jelly-specific trial detail, dose, or route given.
